To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
surfactants and some antibiotics can mitigate the detrimental effect of viruses on bacteria in vitro.
surfactants and bile salts can reduce the detrimental impact of phages in vitro, while antibiotics do not show this effect in most combinations.

the abiotic environmental factors, surfactants and some antibiotics, can mitigate or exacerbate the detrimental effects of phages, and consequently the rate of evolution of phage resistance in bacteria.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the interactions of phages and bacteria in the presence of environmental factors.
understanding how bacteria and phages interact in the presence of other environmental substances.
how bacteria interact with their parasites (viruses) in the natural environment, and how this interaction is modified by compounds that bacteria encounter in nature.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effects of phage on bacterial growth are mitigated by surfactants (SDS and bile salts) but are not affected by antibiotics, excepting a few cases where phages and antibiotics synergize.
the abiotic factors (e.g., antibiotics and surfactants) can modify phages’ impact on bacterial growth.
surfactants and some antibiotics can reduce the impact of phage parasitism, while others can enhance it, and this is a result of the interaction between phage and bacterial growth.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the effects of phages are mitigated by surfactants, while antibiotics can enhance phage‐bacterial interactions.
phages and antibiotics can be antagonists, but not necessarily.
the abiotic environmental context of bacterial–viral interactions has a major impact on bacterial growth and phage‐mediated resistance evolution.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the abiotic conditions of bacterial environments can have a strong effect on phage–bacterial interactions, and that this should be taken into consideration when studying the evolution of bacteria in nature or in the clinic.
the abiotic context in which bacteria and viruses interact can have important effects on the outcomes of these interactions.
the abiotic factors present in the environment can have a significant impact on the interactions between bacteria and their parasitic viruses.
